name: Pre-Order
tagline: A Shopify app that turns out-of-stock or unreleased products into pre-orders, with badges, buttons and order tagging.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The visible part of a pre-order app is small: swap the add-to-cart button when inventory is zero or a release date is in the future, stamp the line item, tag the order, tell the customer when it ships. An agent can build that for one store in a weekend using a custom app token, a metafield per product and a theme snippet, no app store listing required. What does not come for free is everything money-adjacent: deposits and partial payments lean on Shopify's deferred purchase options and selling plans, which is where most of the paid app's actual complexity lives. You also inherit maintenance: Shopify bumps API versions on a schedule and your snippet breaks the day someone changes themes. Fine if you run one store and like editing Liquid, annoying otherwise.
coreLoopDIY: Marks chosen products as pre-order via metafields, rewrites the product page buy button and cart line items accordingly, then tags incoming orders and emails the buyer an expected ship date.
requirements: A Shopify store you admin, with an Online Store 2.0 theme you can edit
A custom app with Admin API access (products, orders, metafields, webhooks)
A public HTTPS endpoint for order webhooks (a small VPS or a tunnel)
SMTP credentials for the pre-order confirmation email
whatYouLose: Deposits, split payments and pay-later flows, which need Shopify selling plans and Shopify Payments rather than a snippet
Per-variant pre-order caps, waitlists and back-in-stock notify flows
Theme compatibility work: the paid app has been beaten against hundreds of themes, yours has been tested against one
Merchant-facing UI, so every rule change is a code change or a metafield edit
Someone else tracking Shopify API deprecations for you
moatNotes: The moat is not the idea, it is living inside Shopify's checkout rules and surviving theme variety.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a store owner's time is worth more than a weekend of Liquid debugging, and because the moment they want a 20 percent deposit instead of a full charge, the DIY version stops being a snippet and starts being a payments integration. Pre-order apps also fail loudly: a broken buy button is lost revenue on the exact products people are most excited about, so paying ten or twenty dollars a month for someone else's regression testing is easy math.
notes: Build it if you want a pre-order button; buy it if you want to take deposits.
prompt:
Build a single-store Shopify pre-order system. No app store listing, no OAuth, no multi-tenant, no telemetry.

Stack: Node 20 with Fastify, plain TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3 for logs, nodemailer for email. Shopify Admin GraphQL API 2024-10 called with a custom app access token. Theme changes as a Liquid snippet plus a small vanilla JS file, no framework in the storefront.

Secrets in .env only: SHOP_DOMAIN, ADMIN_API_TOKEN, WEBHOOK_SECRET, SMTP_URL, FROM_EMAIL.

In scope:
1. A setup script that creates product metafield definitions in namespace preorder: enabled (boolean), release_date (date), message (single_line_text_field), button_label (single_line_text_field).
2. A CLI: 'npm run preorder -- enable --handle some-product --release 2026-11-01' that writes those metafields via metafieldsSet, plus a 'list' command that prints every product currently flagged.
3. A Liquid snippet 'preorder-button.liquid' plus install instructions for the product template: if the product metafield is enabled, or inventory is zero and continue-selling is on, replace the add-to-cart label, show the release message, and add a line item property _preorder_release with the date. Keep it working when JS is off by rendering the label server side in Liquid.
4. A webhook endpoint POST /webhooks/orders-create that verifies the HMAC against WEBHOOK_SECRET, detects any line item carrying _preorder_release, tags the order 'pre-order' and adds an order note listing the affected items, then sends one confirmation email with the earliest release date. Log every processed order id in SQLite and ignore duplicates.
5. A webhook registration script and a health endpoint.

Out of scope, and say so in the README rather than faking it: deposits or partial payments (that requires Shopify selling plans and deferred purchase options), pre-order quantity caps, back-in-stock waitlists, a merchant admin UI, and support for vintage non-2.0 themes.

Deliver: README with exact install steps for the theme snippet, .env.example, the setup and webhook scripts, and one integration test that posts a signed sample order payload and asserts the tag call and the email were attempted.
